title: SUID Binaries: The Root Shell Hiding in Plain Sight
excerpt: A misconfigured SUID bit is one of the fastest paths from a low-privilege shell to root. Here's how the SUID bit works, how attackers find and abuse it, and how to stop it happening on your own boxes.
content:
If you've spent any time on TryHackMe or HackTheBox, you've probably run find / -perm -4000 at some point without fully knowing why it works. This post breaks down the SUID bit from first principles, why it's such a common privilege escalation vector, and how to actually use it — safely, on machines you're authorized to test.

What the SUID Bit Actually Does

Every Linux binary runs with the permissions of the user who launched it — normally. The SUID (Set User ID) bit is an exception. When it's set on an executable, the binary runs with the permissions of the file's owner, not the user who invoked it.

That's the whole mechanism. It exists so that ordinary users can perform specific privileged actions without being handed full root access. The classic example is passwd:

$ ls -l /usr/bin/passwd
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 68208 Jan  1  2026 /usr/bin/passwd

Notice the s where you'd expect an x in the owner's permission triplet. That's the SUID bit. It lets any user change their own password — which requires writing to /etc/shadow, a file only root can touch — without giving them blanket root access. passwd is deliberately, carefully written to only ever touch the one record it should.

Where It Goes Wrong

The problem isn't the SUID bit itself — it's when it ends up on a binary that wasn't designed with that level of trust in mind, or one that's simply powerful enough to be abused. Three common causes:

  • Misconfiguration. An admin sets the SUID bit on a general-purpose tool (find, vim, python3) to work around a permissions headache, not realizing what that tool can do once it's running as root.
  • Legacy or custom binaries. An old in-house tool gets SUID-root so a script can run it, and nobody revisits that decision for years.
  • Vulnerable binaries. A legitimately-SUID program has a bug — a buffer overflow, a path traversal, an unsafe call to system() — that lets you make it do something its author never intended.

Finding SUID Binaries

The standard enumeration command:

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

-perm -4000 matches any file with the SUID bit set, and 2>/dev/null just hides the flood of "permission denied" noise from directories you can't read. On a stock Linux install this returns a fairly predictable list — passwd, su, sudo, mount, ping, and a handful of others. What you're actually looking for is anything unusual in that list: a scripting language interpreter, a text editor, a system utility with more power than its job requires.

GTFOBins: The Cheat Sheet

Once you've got a list of SUID binaries, you don't need to reverse-engineer each one from scratch. GTFOBins is a community-maintained catalog of standard Unix binaries that can be abused to break out of restricted shells or escalate privileges, organized by binary name. Cross-reference your find output against it — if a binary on your list has an entry there tagged for SUID, you likely have a path to root.

A few illustrative examples of the pattern (never run these against a system you don't have explicit authorization to test):

# find(1) with SUID — spawns a root shell via its -exec flag
find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit

# vim(1) with SUID — drop to a privileged shell from within the editor
vim -c ':!/bin/sh'

# python3 with SUID — os.execl inherits the SUID process's privileges
python3 -c 'import os; os.execl("/bin/sh", "sh", "-p")'

The -p flag on /bin/sh matters here — without it, modern shells drop elevated privileges the moment they detect the real and effective UID don't match, as a built-in safety measure.

A Quick Walkthrough

Say you've landed a low-privilege shell on a box during a CTF and enumeration turns up this:

$ find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
/usr/bin/passwd
/usr/bin/su
/usr/bin/mount
/usr/bin/find     <-- not normally SUID

find being SUID is the anomaly worth chasing. Checking GTFOBins confirms it has a known SUID privilege-escalation technique, and the one-liner above hands you a root shell in seconds. That gap — between "here's a weird permission" and "here's exactly how to exploit it" — is precisely the muscle memory OSCP-style labs are designed to build.

Defending Against This

From the blue-team side, the fix is mostly about hygiene:

  • Audit regularly. Run the same find -perm -4000 sweep on your own infrastructure and know exactly why every result is on the list.
  • Set SUID as narrowly as possible. If a script needs elevated privileges for one operation, write a small, purpose-built wrapper instead of granting SUID to a general-purpose tool.
  • Prefer sudo with tight rules over SUID. A carefully scoped sudoers entry is auditable and revocable in a way a SUID bit buried on a filesystem isn't.
  • Automate the check. Tools like linpeas.sh or lynis flag unusual SUID binaries as part of a broader hardening sweep — worth running after any provisioning change.

Takeaway

SUID privilege escalation isn't some exotic zero-day — it's a permission bit doing exactly what it was told to do, on a binary that shouldn't have been trusted with that power. That's what makes it such a reliable entry in the privesc toolkit, and such an easy thing to accidentally introduce as an administrator. Enumerate first, cross-reference against GTFOBins, and understand why each result belongs on the list.
